message.content: {"schema_version":"teaching-unit.v0.4.0","input_manifest_sha256":"cf978d1afdc6e7252750a22fe120d2c58fee464af3d530c5c2446d944a4a52eb","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-or-class-c:lineage:52","source_registry_sha256":"ce8335c1d96ff7ed209bf236ba9a56fe92dfebd915bc0e2fa7fb830ee03f0f09","units":[{"unit_id":"sec06-u01","module_id":"sec06-m01","objective_ids":["sec06-u01"],"title":{"text":"Pedestrians and crosswalk stops","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02","sec06-F03"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Pedestrians and other vulnerable road users are hard to see and have little protection, so most crosswalk rules exist to make you stop early.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"The turn clearance rule changes with whether the intersection has a traffic signal, which is why learners mix the two up.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"You are turning right at a corner with no traffic signal while a pedestrian crosses the street you are turning into.","fact_ids":["sec06-F08"]},"reasoning":{"text":"Without a signal, the pedestrian must clear the lane you are turning into and the next lane before you start.","fact_ids":["sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]},"result":{"text":"You wait until the pedestrian is past both lanes, then make the turn.","fact_ids":["sec06-F08"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking a crosswalk only exists where lines are painted.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11"]},"correction":{"text":"Every intersection has a crosswalk, and an unmarked one is at least six feet wide even with no sidewalk.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Signal means six feet; no signal means two lanes clear.","fact_ids":["sec06-R20"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"At a corner with a traffic light, how far must a crossing pedestrian be from the lane you are turning into before you turn?","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]},"answer":{"text":"At least six feet.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07"]},"rationale":{"text":"With a signal the clearance is six feet from your target lane; the two-lane rule is for intersections without a signal.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R20"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who needs your extra care","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Vulnerable road users are hard to see.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},{"text":"Most have no crash protection.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson is about the people who share the road with you but have almost nothing protecting them. The manual calls them vulnerable road users, and the list is wider than many drivers expect. It includes pedestrians, bicyclists and motorcyclists, but also highway workers and anyone on a skateboard, scooter or similar device in a public way, a crosswalk or on a highway shoulder. They are vulnerable for two simple reasons: they can be hard to see, and in a crash they usually have no protection from injury. Keep that picture in mind as we go through the crosswalk rules.","fact_ids":["sec06-F01","sec06-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"What counts as a pedestrian","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Walking or rolling both count.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},{"text":"Crossing starts when any part enters the road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"In the Oregon manual the word pedestrian covers more than people on foot. Someone rolling on a skateboard, a scooter or in a wheelchair is a pedestrian too. The moment a pedestrian counts as crossing is also earlier than many people think. As soon as any part of the person, or something they are using, such as a cane, a wheelchair or a bicycle, moves onto the road, that person is legally crossing. And you must stop for a pedestrian crossing at any crosswalk, whether the crosswalk is marked with paint or not. A cane or wheelchair touching the road counts.","fact_ids":["sec06-F03","sec06-F04","sec06-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Which lanes make you stop","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F10","sec06-R21"]},"lines":[{"text":"Your lane or the lane beside it.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F10","sec06-R21"]},{"text":"The lane you are turning into.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F10","sec06-R21"]},{"text":"Not beyond a safety island.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F10","sec06-R21"]}],"narration":{"text":"So when exactly do you stop and stay stopped? Look at where the pedestrian is. If they are in your lane, in the lane next to yours, and a bike lane beside you counts as that lane, or in the lane you are turning into, you stop and you remain stopped. There is one exception the manual spells out. If the pedestrian is in a crosswalk on the far side of a safety island, you do not have to stop. The island divides the crossing, so the duty to stop belongs to the traffic on the pedestrian's side of the island. When in doubt about the lane, stop and wait.","fact_ids":["sec06-F06","sec06-F10","sec06-R21"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Turning past a pedestrian","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]},"lines":[{"text":"With a signal: six feet clear.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]},{"text":"No signal: target lane and next lane clear.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]}],"narration":{"text":"Turning is where the timing gets precise. At an intersection with a traffic signal, the pedestrian must be at least six feet from the lane you are turning into before you begin the turn. At an intersection without a signal, the bar is higher. The pedestrian must have cleared the lane you are turning into and the next lane as well. Picture a driver at a quiet corner with no light, eager to turn because the walker is almost across one lane. That is too early. With no signal, you wait until two lanes are clear before you start to move.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-F08","sec06-R20"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The stopped car trap","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F04"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never pass a car stopped at a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F04"]},{"text":"Someone may be crossing out of sight.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a trap that catches drivers in multi-lane traffic. The car in the next lane has stopped at a crosswalk, and your lane looks open, so you roll past. That is illegal. The driver who stopped may be waiting for a pedestrian you cannot see, and that pedestrian may step right into your path from in front of the stopped car. The rule is simple and absolute: you never pass a vehicle that is stopped at a crosswalk. Treat a stopped car at a crosswalk as a warning that someone is crossing, even when you cannot see them yourself.","fact_ids":["sec06-F09","sec06-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s6","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Finding unmarked crosswalks","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Every intersection has a crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13"]},{"text":"Picture the sidewalk carried across.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13"]},{"text":"At least six feet wide.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Many crosswalks have no paint at all, and they still count. Every intersection has a crosswalk, even without painted lines. To find an unmarked one, imagine the sidewalk or shoulder at the corner continuing straight across the road. That imagined strip is the crosswalk, and it is at least six feet wide. It exists even where there is no sidewalk or shoulder to extend. Between intersections you may also meet a mid-block crosswalk, and it may have a flashing yellow light that warns you a pedestrian is crossing or is about to cross.","fact_ids":["sec06-F11","sec06-F12","sec06-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s7","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check on turning","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R20","sec06-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Signal at the corner.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R20","sec06-F08"]},{"text":"How much clearance?","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R20","sec06-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are turning at a corner that has a traffic light, and a pedestrian is crossing the street you are turning into. How far must that pedestrian be from the lane you are turning into before you start your turn? The answer is at least six feet. Remember that this six-foot rule is the signalized case. If the same corner had no signal, you would wait longer, until the pedestrian had cleared your target lane and the next lane too. Mixing those two up is the most common slip on this topic, so tie six feet to the signal.","fact_ids":["sec06-F07","sec06-R20","sec06-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u01-s8","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Keep crosswalks clear","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F06"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never stop over the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F06"]},{"text":"Stop before sidewalks at driveways.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F06"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two last habits protect people on foot. First, when you stop, keep every part of your vehicle out of the crosswalk. A car sitting over the crosswalk forces pedestrians to walk around it, often out into moving traffic. Second, when you cross a sidewalk to get into or out of a parking lot, an alley or a driveway, stop before you reach the sidewalk and yield to pedestrians and bicyclists. Put together with the lane rules and the turn clearances, these habits mean you stop early, wait long enough, and never leave a walker stranded in danger.","fact_ids":["sec06-F14","sec06-F15","sec06-F06"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u02","module_id":"sec06-m02","objective_ids":["sec06-u02"],"title":{"text":"School zones and white canes","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-F17","sec06-F18"]},"why_how":[{"text":"School zone rules depend on which sign is posted, so knowing each sign tells you exactly when the lower limit applies.","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F20","sec06-F21"]},{"text":"Blind pedestrians and children may not see or judge traffic, so the manual asks you to stay stopped longer for them.","fact_ids":["sec06-F23","sec06-F25"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"On a Saturday afternoon you pass a school speed sign for when children are present, and two children are waiting at the crosswalk.","fact_ids":["sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A children-present sign applies on any day at any hour that children are present, and children waiting at a crosswalk count.","fact_ids":["sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]},"result":{"text":"You slow to the school limit of twenty miles per hour even though it is the weekend.","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F21"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking every school speed sign only applies during school hours.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22"]},"correction":{"text":"Only the school-hours sign is tied to set hours on school days; the children-present sign applies whenever children are present.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22","sec06-F20","sec06-F21"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Clock sign follows the school day; kids sign follows the kids.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"A school-hours sign is posted and you cannot tell whether school is in session today. What do you do?","fact_ids":["sec06-F20"]},"answer":{"text":"Slow to twenty miles per hour.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20"]},"rationale":{"text":"The manual says that when you are unsure whether it is a school day, you slow to the school limit.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Slowing down for schools","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},"lines":[{"text":"School zones are marked by signs.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},{"text":"The sign type decides when to slow.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]}],"narration":{"text":"School zones are one of the places where a single sign changes your speed, so it pays to know exactly what each sign means. A school zone is a stretch of road beside a school or a school crosswalk that signs mark as a school zone. The start of the zone is shown by a yellow five-sided sign, which also warns of school crossings. When you see that shape, start looking for children and be ready to stop. In this lesson we will separate the school speed signs, then cover pedestrians with white canes or guide dogs, and children at play.","fact_ids":["sec06-F16","sec06-F17"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The school speed zone","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F19"]},"lines":[{"text":"Twenty miles per hour.","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F19"]},{"text":"From the school limit sign to the end sign.","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F19"]}],"narration":{"text":"Inside a school speed zone the limit drops to twenty miles per hour. The zone begins at the school speed limit sign that shows twenty, and it ends at the END SCHOOL ZONE sign or at another posted speed sign. Some school speed signs carry a yellow light. When that light is flashing, children are arriving at school or leaving it, and the reduced limit applies. So a flashing light is not a decoration or a general caution. It tells you the twenty mile per hour limit is in force right now, and you should already be at that speed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F18","sec06-F19"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Two kinds of school signs","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-F21","sec06-F22","sec06-R22"]},"lines":[{"text":"School hours: set times on school days.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-F21","sec06-F22","sec06-R22"]},{"text":"Children present: any day, any hour.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-F21","sec06-F22","sec06-R22"]}],"narration":{"text":"Two school speed signs look similar but work differently. The school-hours sign applies from seven in the morning to five in the afternoon on days when school is in session. If you are not sure whether it is a school day, you slow to twenty anyway. The children-present sign is not tied to the clock at all. It applies on any day and at any hour that children are present. The manual defines present: children waiting at a crosswalk, children in or walking through a crosswalk, or a traffic patrol member there to help them cross.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-F21","sec06-F22","sec06-R22"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The weekend school sign trap","fact_ids":["sec06-R22","sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]},"lines":[{"text":"Weekend does not cancel children present.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22","sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]},{"text":"Check which sign is posted.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22","sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. A driver passes a school on a weekend evening and assumes school signs do not count when school is closed. That is only true for the school-hours sign, which covers set hours on school days. If the sign says the limit applies when children are present, the day and the hour do not matter. Children waiting at the crosswalk on a Saturday trigger the twenty mile per hour limit just as they would on a Tuesday morning. Before you decide a school sign does not apply, read which kind it is, then look for children.","fact_ids":["sec06-R22","sec06-F21","sec06-F22"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"White canes and guide dogs","fact_ids":["sec06-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Yield and stop.","fact_ids":["sec06-F23"]},{"text":"Stay stopped until the whole road is crossed.","fact_ids":["sec06-F23"]},{"text":"Even on a green light.","fact_ids":["sec06-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"A pedestrian with limited vision, or one who is blind or deaf and blind and is using a white cane or a guide dog, gets your full patience. You yield to that person. If they are crossing or about to cross, you stop, and you stay stopped until they have crossed the whole road. That last part matters: not just your lane, the entire road. And it holds even when your light is green. A green light gives you the right to proceed only when the way is clear, and here it is not clear until that pedestrian has finished crossing.","fact_ids":["sec06-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check on school signs","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-R22","sec06-F21"]},"lines":[{"text":"School-hours sign.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-R22","sec06-F21"]},{"text":"Not sure it is a school day?","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-R22","sec06-F21"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are driving past a school with a school-hours speed sign, and you honestly cannot tell whether school is in session today. What should you do? The answer is to slow to twenty miles per hour. The manual gives that exact instruction for uncertainty, so you never have to guess. Compare it with the children-present sign, which does not depend on the school calendar at all; it applies whenever children are present, any day, at any hour. Matching the right rule to the right sign is what this topic tests.","fact_ids":["sec06-F20","sec06-R22","sec06-F21"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u02-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Children near the road","fact_ids":["sec06-F24","sec06-F25","sec06-F23"]},"lines":[{"text":"Watch for kids behind parked cars.","fact_ids":["sec06-F24","sec06-F25","sec06-F23"]},{"text":"Wait for children to clear crosswalks.","fact_ids":["sec06-F24","sec06-F25","sec06-F23"]}],"narration":{"text":"Children are unpredictable, so the manual adds two habits. In neighborhoods and near parks, keep away from parked cars that block your view, and take great care when backing out of a driveway, because children may be playing behind your vehicle. At crosswalks, stop and yield when children step in or when a school crossing guard signals you, and stay stopped until the children are out of the crosswalk. Put that together with the school signs and the white cane rule, and the theme of this lesson is clear: around children and blind pedestrians, you wait longer.","fact_ids":["sec06-F24","sec06-F25","sec06-F23"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":39,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec06-u03","module_id":"sec06-m03","objective_ids":["sec06-u03"],"title":{"text":"Bicycles and bike boxes","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27","sec06-F28"]},"why_how":[{"text":"Bicyclists are hard to see and react to road hazards that drivers barely notice, so they need extra room.","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27"]},{"text":"Bike lanes, bike boxes and passing at higher speeds come with specific rules that are easy to get wrong.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F30"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"You are waiting at a red light with a green painted box ahead of the stop line, and you want to turn right.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A bike box means you stop behind the box, and right turns on red are not allowed at that intersection.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34"]},"result":{"text":"You wait behind the box for green, then signal and yield to bicyclists on your right before turning.","fact_ids":["sec06-F34"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking you can drive in a bike lane to set up a right turn.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28"]},"correction":{"text":"You never drive or park in a bike lane; crossing it is allowed only to turn or to get into or out of an alley, driveway or private road.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Cross the bike lane, never cruise it.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"You are traveling faster than thirty-five miles per hour behind a bicyclist in your lane. What must be true before you pass?","fact_ids":["sec06-F30"]},"answer":{"text":"You must leave enough distance that you would not hit the rider if they fell.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30"]},"rationale":{"text":"At speeds above thirty-five miles per hour, the manual allows the pass only with room to miss a falling rider.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Sharing the road with bicyclists","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27"]},"lines":[{"text":"Riders are hard to see.","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27"]},{"text":"Hazards can push them into your path.","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27"]}],"narration":{"text":"Bicyclists share most roads with you, and they are easy to miss. They are harder to see than other vehicles, and a rider can sit hidden in your blind spot. They also react to things a driver hardly notices. Potholes, glass, litter, storm grates and railroad tracks can make a rider slow down or swerve, and so can a car door that suddenly opens. Any of these can move a bicyclist into your path. That is why the manual asks you to leave riders plenty of room, and why every rule in this lesson is about space and yielding.","fact_ids":["sec06-F26","sec06-F27"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Bike lane rules","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F32"]},"lines":[{"text":"Never drive or park in a bike lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F32"]},{"text":"Cross it only to turn or enter.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F32"]},{"text":"Yield before turning across.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F32"]}],"narration":{"text":"A bike lane is not extra road for cars. You may never drive in it or park in it. You may cross it, but only to make a turn or to get into or out of an alley, a driveway or a private road. Before you turn across a bike lane, or across a sidewalk, you must yield to any bicyclist using it. And at intersections you yield to bicyclists exactly as you would to any other vehicle. The same respect extends to motorized wheelchairs, scooters and personal assistive mobility devices, which may use bike lanes and paths; you yield to them like riders.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F32"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Passing a bicyclist","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},"lines":[{"text":"Ordinary passing rules apply.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},{"text":"Above thirty-five: room for a fall.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},{"text":"Cannot pass safely? Stay behind.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]}],"narration":{"text":"Passing a rider follows the same passing rules you use for any vehicle, plus one extra condition at higher speeds. When you are going faster than thirty-five miles per hour, you may pass a bicyclist in your lane only if you leave enough distance that you would not hit the rider if they fell. Think of the space a person needs if they tip over sideways, and leave at least that. If oncoming traffic or a curve means you cannot pass safely, the answer is not to squeeze by. You slow down and stay behind the rider until a safe pass opens up.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":41,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"The bike lane turn trap","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F26"]},"lines":[{"text":"Do not merge into the bike lane early.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F26"]},{"text":"Yield to the rider, then turn.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F26"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a common trap. A driver planning a right turn drifts into the bike lane well before the corner, the way cars sometimes move to the curb. In Oregon that is not allowed. You may cross a bike lane to turn, but you may not drive in it to get ready for the turn. The right move is to stay in your lane, check your mirror and blind spot for a rider coming up in the bike lane, yield to that rider, and only then turn across the bike lane. Crossing is allowed; cruising along in it is not. The rider in the bike lane always goes first.","fact_ids":["sec06-F28","sec06-F29","sec06-F26"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s5","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Bike boxes and sharrows","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F35"]},"lines":[{"text":"Stop behind the green box.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F35"]},{"text":"No right turn on red there.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F35"]},{"text":"Chevrons mean a shared lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F35"]}],"narration":{"text":"Some intersections have a bike box, usually a green painted box marked with a white bicycle symbol, sitting ahead of the car stop line. At a signal you stop behind the box, never inside it, and bicyclists move into the box in front of you. At those intersections right turns on a red light are not allowed, and when you turn right on green you signal and yield to bicyclists on your right. Elsewhere you may see a sharrow, two chevrons painted above a bicycle symbol. It marks a shared lane where bicyclists may be riding in the road with you.","fact_ids":["sec06-F33","sec06-F34","sec06-F35"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":40,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec06-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Quick check on passing","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},"lines":[{"text":"Faster than thirty-five.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]},{"text":"Rider in your lane.","fact_ids":["sec06-F30","sec06-F31"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are traveling faster than thirty-five miles per hour, and a bicyclist is riding ahead of you in your lane. What has to be true before you pass? The answer is that you must leave enough distance that you would not hit the rider if they fell. That is the extra condition for higher speeds, layered on top of the ordinary passing rules.
